why: The world's best striped marlin fly and light-tackle fishery during the fall bait-ball season, with record days of 40-plus fish on fly.
heads_up: Mothership or long runs offshore; October storms can cancel trips

name: Magpie River
why: Fly-in multi-day with big class IV and the Magpie Falls finale; ranked among the world's top ten rafting rivers and granted legal personhood in 2021.
heads_up: Float-plane access only; expedition-grade

name: Main Salmon (River of No Return)
why: Eighty miles of sandy beaches and class III-IV from Corn Creek through the Frank Church, a family multi-day staple with a permit lottery.
heads_up: Permit lottery Jun-Sep; long shuttle

name: Makaha
why: Site of the Makaha International, the first major surf contest (1954), and the heart of west-side Hawaiian surf culture.
heads_up: Strong local community; respect etiquette; big-wave backwash in winter

name: Makapuu
why: Oahu's iconic trade-wind cliff site flown since the 1970s with a strong local club and spectacular ridge runs to Waimanalo.
heads_up: Strong trade winds and turbulence; experts with local intro; HPA membership

name: Malibu / Surfrider Beach
why: The world's first World Surfing Reserve and the longboard wave that defined 1960s surf culture.
heads_up: Extremely crowded; water quality issues after rain; paid parking

name: Maliko Run
why: The world's most famous downwind SUP run, 9 miles from Maliko Gulch to Kahului with 20-25 knot trades and the OluKai Ho'olaule'a race.
heads_up: Open ocean and shipping; one-way shuttle; experienced paddlers only

name: Mammoth Mountain
why: 11,053 ft summit, Unbound terrain parks and seasons that routinely run into summer, plus a pioneering lift-served bike park.
heads_up: High winds close the top; long drive from LA

name: Manasquan Inlet
why: New Jersey's premier wave, a hollow inlet jetty peak that anchors the Jersey Shore surf scene.
heads_up: Beach badges in summer; cold winter water; jetty rocks

name: Maple Canyon
why: Unique cobblestone conglomerate sport climbing with hundreds of steep routes in a shady canyon.
heads_up: Popular campground; afternoon shade only on some walls

name: Marblehead
why: Marblehead Race Week (since 1889) and the Marblehead-to-Halifax race make this one of the oldest racing harbours in the Americas.
heads_up: Rocky coast; few guest moorings

name: Margaree River
why: Cape Breton's fly-only Atlantic salmon river with a strong fall run, the Margaree Salmon Museum and public pools.
heads_up: Fly-only; low summer water; fall weather

name: Marin / Mount Tamalpais
why: Birthplace of mountain biking (Repack, Gary Fisher, Joe Breeze) with Camp Tamarancho and China Camp as the legal singletrack.
heads_up: Most Mt Tam singletrack is closed to bikes; Tamarancho needs a day pass

name: Marmot Basin
why: Jasper National Park's uncrowded resort with 3,000 ft of vertical and Canada's highest base elevation.
heads_up: Cold and remote; Jasper recovering from the 2024 wildfire

name: Maroon Bells / Four Pass Loop
why: The 26-mile Four Pass Loop over four 12,000 ft passes is Colorado's most famous backpacking circuit.
heads_up: Shuttle and overnight permits required; altitude and storms

name: Marquette
why: Upper Peninsula trail town with the Noquemanon South Trails network, Marquette Mountain lift-served riding and the Ore to Shore race.
heads_up: Black flies in early summer

name: Marshall Peak / Crestline (Andy Jackson Airpark)
why: The most-flown mountain site in the US with the Crestline Soaring Society, shuttle service, 750 ft to 1000 m launches and a club-owned landing field.
heads_up: AJX is the only legal landing in the valley; shuttle fee and CSS membership; summer midday turbulence

name: Maui Channel (Lanai to Kaanapali)
why: The Maui Channel Swim, the original open-water masters relay since 1972, crosses the Auau Channel from Lanai to Kaanapali Beach with escort boats.
heads_up: Open-ocean swells and current; escort boat required

name: Mavericks
why: The most famous big-wave break on the US mainland, with a long-running invitational contest and a dedicated big-wave community off Pillar Point.
heads_up: Experts only; 25-60 ft faces, rocks, cold water and sharks

name: Mazatlán
why: Historic billfish port with one of Mexico's oldest sportfishing fleets, known for striped marlin and sailfish numbers.
heads_up: Summer heat and storms; long offshore runs

name: Mendocino Coast (Van Damme)
why: Van Damme State Park's protected cove opens onto sea caves and arches, with guided tours and the Mendocino sea-kayak community.
heads_up: Cold water and fog; swell closes caves

name: Middle Fork Salmon
why: One hundred miles of free-flowing class III-IV with hot springs through the Frank Church Wilderness; the most coveted permit lottery in the US after the Grand Canyon.
heads_up: Permit lottery; fly-in from Boundary Creek at low water

name: Mingan Archipelago
why: Limestone monoliths, puffins and whales across a national park reserve accessible only by boat, with Parks Canada-recognized operators.
heads_up: Cold Gulf water and exposed crossings

name: Mingus Mountain
why: Arizona's premier free-flight site with the Arizona Hang Gliding and Paragliding Association, drive-up launch at 7,800 ft and Verde Valley XC.
heads_up: Strong desert thermals; AZHPA membership and site intro; hot summers

name: Miramichi River
why: The most productive Atlantic salmon river in North America, with historic lodges, the Atlantic Salmon Museum and a fall run of 30 lb fish.
heads_up: Non-residents must fish with a licensed guide; catch-and-release rules change yearly

name: Mirror Lake
why: The Ironman Lake Placid swim lake, with a permanent underwater cable course that makes it one of the most-swum open-water training venues in the US.
heads_up: Crowded along the cable; motorboats banned

name: Mission Bay, San Diego
why: A 4,600-acre flatwater aquatic park with multiple SUP outfitters and the long-running Hanohano Huki Ocean Challenge race.
heads_up: Boat traffic in channels; afternoon westerly wind

name: Missouri River (Craig)
why: Below Holter Dam the 'Mo' is a giant spring creek with huge rainbow numbers and a town of fly shops and guides built around it.
heads_up: Crowded; wind; drift-boat traffic at Craig

name: Misty Fjords
why: Rudyerd Bay and Walker Cove's 3,000-foot walls, reached by floatplane or boat from Ketchikan, are Southeast Alaska's classic multi-day paddle.
heads_up: Heavy rain, floatplane access, few landings

name: Moab
why: The original MTB pilgrimage: Slickrock, Porcupine Rim, The Whole Enchilada, Amasa Back, Kokopelli and the Moab Brand trails.
heads_up: Exposure and heat; carry extra water, respect cryptobiotic soil

name: Mokuleia
why: Oahu's North Shore kite beach, with cross-shore trades and a long shallow reef lagoon used by the island's advanced riders.
heads_up: Winter swell and rip currents; reef is shallow

name: Molokini Crater
why: A crescent-shaped crater marine sanctuary off Maui with 150-ft visibility, the most-visited snorkel and dive site in Hawaii.
heads_up: Morning boats only; Back Wall dive is advanced

name: Mont Yamaska
why: Montreal's most-flown site with multiple launches and local schools, managed by the Association Québécoise de Vol Libre.
heads_up: AQVL membership; private land access rules

name: Mont-Saint-Pierre
why: Quebec's free-flight capital, home of the Fête du Vol Libre since 1978, with summit launches at 430 m above the St. Lawrence.
heads_up: 4x4 bus or hike to launch; sea breeze and coastal weather; remote

name: Mont-Sainte-Anne
why: Quebec City's premier mountain, host of World Cup skiing and the longest-running UCI Mountain Bike World Cup venue in the world, with gondola-lapped rock-garden downhill.
heads_up: Rocky, technical DH; limited beginner terrain

name: Mont-Tremblant
why: Eastern Canada's flagship resort since 1939, consistently rated the top ski resort in the East by SKI readers.
heads_up: Extreme cold snaps; very busy pedestrian village

name: Montauk
why: The East Coast's surfcasting mecca, with the fall striped bass and false albacore blitz under Montauk Light.
heads_up: Slippery rocks and crowds in the fall run; sudden weather

name: Montauk / Ditch Plains
why: Long Island's surf capital, a longboard-friendly reef at Ditch Plains with a deep-rooted surf community.
heads_up: Resident parking permits in summer; very crowded; hurricane swell

name: Monterey Bay / Elkhorn Slough
why: Sea otters, seals and sea lions at close range in Elkhorn Slough and off Cannery Row make this the most reliable wildlife paddling in California.
heads_up: Afternoon wind; keep distance from otters under federal rules

name: Monterey Breakwater (San Carlos Beach)
why: The most-dived site on the US West Coast, a sheltered kelp forest with sea otters and harbor seals inside Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary.
heads_up: Cold (50s F), thick wetsuit or drysuit; surge in winter

name: Montrose Beach
why: Chicago's only sanctioned city kite beach, with Park District rules, Wilson and Montrose launch corridors and a committed local crew.
heads_up: Only on red/yellow flag days; PFD required; cold water

name: Moraine Lake / Larch Valley
why: Larch Valley and Sentinel Pass above Moraine Lake are Banff's most famous fall hikes.
heads_up: Shuttle-only access, no private cars; group-of-four grizzly rule

name: Morehead City / Graveyard of the Atlantic (U-352)
why: World-famous wreck diving on the U-352 submarine, the Spar and the Aeolus, with sand tiger sharks on nearly every wreck and a well-established charter fleet.
heads_up: Long offshore runs, 100-ft depths, Gulf Stream current

name: Morningside Flight Park
why: New England's main training flight park with a 450 ft hill, school, towing and an active community since the 1970s.
heads_up: Short flights unless soarable; mostly a school hill

name: Mosquito Lagoon
why: The 'Redfish Capital of the World' with sight-fishing for giant redfish and seatrout in clear shallow water inside Canaveral National Seashore.
heads_up: Spooky fish in skinny water; seagrass loss in recent years; manatee zones

name: Mount Bohemia
why: No groomers, no beginners, 273 inches of lake-effect snow and a cult reputation that has it voted among North America's best.
heads_up: Remote Keweenaw tip; expert-only terrain

name: Mount Lemmon
venueType: granite crags along a mountain highway
why: The Catalina Highway stacks 2,000+ routes across elevation bands, letting Tucson climb year-round; Windy Point is the hub.
heads_up: Summer heat below 6,000 ft; winter snow on top

name: Mount Rainier
why: The most-climbed glaciated peak in the US (Disappointment Cleaver, Emmons) and home of the 93-mile Wonderland Trail and Skyline day hike.
heads_up: Climbing permits and glacier skills required; Wonderland permits by lottery

name: Mount Washington Bike Park
why: Vancouver Island's only lift-served bike park with a long history of BC Cup downhill racing.
heads_up: Short season; weekends only in shoulder weeks

name: Mount Whitney
why: Highest peak in the Lower 48 with the 22-mile Whitney Trail, the Mountaineer's Route and classic East Face alpine rock climbs.
heads_up: Permit lottery; altitude (14,505 ft)

name: Mount Woodside
why: Vancouver's main mountain site with two groomed launches and a long Fraser Valley flying history under the West Coast Soaring Club.
heads_up: Riverside LZ landing pass required; FSR access; westerly valley wind afternoons

name: Mountain Creek Bike Park
why: Birthplace of the US Open of Mountain Biking (2003) and the closest rocky lift-served downhill to New York City.
heads_up: Rocky, rough trails; full-face recommended

name: Mt. Bachelor
why: A 9,000 ft volcano with 360-degree summit skiing, Oregon's largest ski area and a season into late May.
heads_up: Summit lift often closed by wind and rime

name: Mt. Baker
why: World-record 1,140-inch season (1998-99), the Legendary Banked Slalom and a snowboard-history pedigree second to none.
heads_up: Deep, wet snow; serious slackcountry avalanche terrain

name: Mt. Hood (Timberline & Meadows)
why: Timberline runs North America's only near year-round lift skiing on the Palmer snowfield (home of summer race and freestyle camps), and the 40-mile Timberline Trail circles the volcano from the lodge.
heads_up: Summer skiing is mornings only; glacial river fords on the Timberline Trail

name: Mussel Rock
why: The Bay Area's main coastal soaring site, flown daily on the sea breeze with the Fellow Feathers club and nearby schools.
heads_up: Strong afternoon winds and rotor behind the cliff; narrow beach landing with tide timing

name: Nā Pali Coast / Kalalau Trail
why: The 11-mile Kalalau Trail along the Nā Pali cliffs is Hawaii's most famous and most permit-restricted hike, and the summer-only 17-mile Haena-to-Polihale paddle beneath the same cliffs is regarded as the premier sea-kayak day trip in the US.
heads_up: Hāʻena State Park entry and camping permits; Crawler's Ledge exposure; kayaking summer-only with surf landings

name: Nahanni River
why: Fly-in from Virginia Falls through four canyons of the UNESCO-listed Nahanni National Park Reserve; Canada's definitive river expedition.
heads_up: Float-plane access; Parks Canada registration and licensed outfitters

name: Nanaimo artificial reefs
why: Home of the HMCS Saskatchewan, HMCS Cape Breton and the Rivtow Lion, the biggest artificial-reef cluster in Canada, plus the Snake Island sea-lion wall.
heads_up: Cold water, current on the wrecks; best viz in winter

name: Nantahala River
why: Home of the Nantahala Outdoor Center and the 2013 Freestyle Worlds; the reliable class II-III release run is where much of the Southeast learns to paddle.
heads_up: Very cold bottom-release water year-round; busy summer rafting traffic

name: Nantucket
why: Nantucket Race Week and the Opera House Cup classic-yacht regatta anchor a celebrated August sailing scene.
heads_up: Shoals around the island; fog

name: Narragansett / Point Judith
why: New England's surf town, with Narragansett Town Beach for learners and Point Judith's reefs for experts, and surf shops dating to the 1960s.
heads_up: Paid beach entry in summer; cold water; hurricane swells

name: Nelson
why: Legendary steep Kootenay loam (Mountain Station, Morning Mountain) and the home of freeride pros like Kurt Sorge.
heads_up: Steep, technical and shuttle-dependent

name: Nenana River
why: Glacial class III-IV in the Nenana Canyon at the Denali park entrance, Alaska's most-rafted river.
heads_up: Silty 38°F water; drysuits mandatory

name: Nevado de Toluca
why: The crater lagoons at 4,200 m and the Pico del Fraile ridge are the most accessible high-altitude hike from Mexico City.
heads_up: Altitude; vehicles stop below the crater, walk in

name: New River Gorge
venueType: sandstone cliffs and class III-IV gorge
why: Over 1,600 hard sandstone trad and sport routes on Endless Wall plus the Lower New's big-volume class III-IV, the East's most-rafted summer run, all based from Fayetteville.
heads_up: High spring flows push the river to class V; stiff climbing grades; crowded summer weekends

name: New Smyrna Beach
why: The most consistent surf in Florida at the Ponce Inlet jetty, with a thriving local pro scene.
heads_up: 'Shark bite capital of the world' with frequent minor bites; drive-on beach

name: Newport
why: America's sailing capital: America's Cup home for 53 years, the Newport Bermuda Race start, Sail Newport at Fort Adams and a summer-long regatta calendar.
heads_up: Crowded harbour and moorings in July

name: Newport Beach / Balboa
why: Start of the Newport-to-Ensenada race (since 1948, billed as the world's largest international yacht race) and home of Newport Harbor Yacht Club.
heads_up: Crowded harbour; light morning wind

name: Niihau / Lehua Rock
why: Kauai's premier dive: summer-only boat trips across the channel to Lehua and Niihau for monk seals, pelagics and 100-ft-plus visibility.
heads_up: Rough channel crossing; summer season only; advanced

name: Nitinat Lake
why: A brackish Vancouver Island lake with a mid-morning-to-sunset thermal that locals claim is the most consistent 20+ kn wind in North America, with a lakeside campground run by the Ditidaht Nation.
heads_up: Logging roads, no cell service, rocky barnacle launch

name: Nolichucky Gorge
why: Deepest gorge in the East outside the Smokies, with a spring class III-IV run and a long-standing rafting base at Erwin.
heads_up: Rain-dependent; railroad-only access through the gorge

name: North Cascades (Cascade Pass / Maple Pass)
why: Cascade Pass-Sahale Arm and the Maple Pass Loop are the North Cascades' signature glacier-view hikes.
heads_up: Rough access road; snow on passes into July

name: North Shore (Fromme / Seymour / Cypress)
why: Birthplace of North Shore freeride; woodwork, roots and rock on Mt Fromme, Seymour and Cypress maintained by the NSMBA.
heads_up: Very technical, slick in rain; climb up Mountain Highway

name: North Umpqua River
why: Thirty-one miles of fly-only water made famous by Zane Grey; the classic summer steelhead swing river of the Pacific Northwest.
heads_up: Slick bedrock wading; fly-only regulations; wild-fish release

name: Northstar Bike Park
why: Tahoe's lift-served gravity park, known for steep, loose, rocky DH and the Livewire jump trail.
heads_up: Loose decomposed granite; expert-leaning

name: Oahu wrecks (Sea Tiger, YO-257)
why: Oahu's charter fleet runs daily to the Sea Tiger, YO-257 and San Pedro wrecks off Waikiki, plus the Corsair, among the best wreck dives in the Pacific.
heads_up: Depths 80-130 ft; current

name: Oakridge
why: IMBA Gold Ride Center and 'Mountain Biking Capital of the Northwest' with Alpine, Middle Fork Willamette and McKenzie River.
heads_up: Long shuttle days; limited services

name: Obed Wild and Scenic River
why: NPS-managed steep sandstone sport climbing at Lilly Bluff and the Obed river gorge, a Southeast staple.
heads_up: Slippery river-gorge approaches; no bolting without permit

name: Ocean Beach, San Francisco
why: San Francisco's city beach break, known for heavy winter swells and a strong year-round surf community; hosted the Rip Curl Pro in 2011.
heads_up: Powerful rips and long paddle-outs; cold water; not for beginners

name: Ocoee River
why: Site of the 1996 Olympic whitewater slalom; the Middle Ocoee's continuous class III-IV and scheduled TVA releases make it the most-rafted river in the US.
heads_up: Release schedule only; Upper (Olympic) section runs limited summer weekends

name: Ogden Point Breakwater
why: Victoria's classic shore dive along a kilometre of breakwater wall packed with anemones, wolf eels and octopus, with a dive centre on the pier.
heads_up: Cold; current at the end of the breakwater

name: Okanagan Lake / Kelowna
why: BC's warm-water paddling destination with the Kelowna Paddle Centre and a lakeshore of rental outfitters, and host of the Across the Lake Swim, Canada's largest and longest-running open-water swim (since 1949).
heads_up: Afternoon wind and chop; boat traffic near marinas

name: Old Rag / Shenandoah
why: Old Rag's boulder scramble is the Mid-Atlantic's most famous day hike, with Skyline Drive and the AT running through Shenandoah.
heads_up: Day-use ticket required Mar–Nov; crowds

name: Olympic National Park (Hoh / Hurricane Ridge)
why: The Hoh River to Glacier Meadows, Enchanted Valley and Hurricane Ridge span rainforest, river and alpine hiking in one park.
heads_up: Wilderness permits; constant rain outside summer

name: Olympic Peninsula Steelhead Rivers
why: The Hoh, Sol Duc, Bogachiel and Queets are the last great wild winter steelhead rivers in the lower 48, with a dedicated Spey community.
heads_up: Constant rain and blown-out rivers; evolving wild-steelhead closures; check WDFW rules

name: Ottawa River
why: Warm, huge-volume Main and Middle channels from McCoy's Chute, home of Wilderness Tours, OWL and the Freestyle Worlds; North America's best big-water playboating.
heads_up: Pay take-out at outfitters; big holes like Phil's

name: Outer Banks (Hatteras)
why: Cape Point surf casting for drum and the Hatteras offshore fleet for billfish and tuna make the OBX the East Coast's fishing hub.
heads_up: ORV beach permits; weather and Diamond Shoals seas

name: Owens Valley (Walt's Point)
why: Legendary big-air XC venue where many distance records were set; launches at 9,000 ft off the Sierra escarpment.
heads_up: Violent thermals and dust devils; experts only; high altitude

name: Pacific City / Cape Kiwanda
why: Oregon's most visited surf beach, sheltered by Cape Kiwanda with a surf shop, rentals and lessons on the sand.
heads_up: Cold water year-round (5/4 wetsuit); summer weekend crowds

name: Pacific Crest Trail (Southern Terminus)
why: The Mexican border monument at Campo is where the 2,650-mile PCT begins; the thru-hike is the most famous in North America.
heads_up: Long-distance permit quota; desert water carries

name: Palisades Tahoe
why: 1960 Olympic host and the home of extreme-ski cinema: KT-22, the Palisades and 6,000 acres linked with Alpine Meadows.
heads_up: Sierra cement after warm storms; weekend Bay Area traffic

name: Panama City Beach wrecks
why: Self-styled Wreck Capital of the South with the Black Bart, Empire Mica, bridge spans and dozens of artificial reefs served by a mature charter fleet.
heads_up: Summer thunderstorms; deeper wrecks need advanced cert

name: Park City Mountain
why: The largest lift-served ski area in the US by acreage, 2002 Olympic venue, with an IMBA Gold-level summer trail town.
heads_up: High altitude (7,000-9,500 ft); afternoon storms

name: Payette River (North Fork, South Fork, Main)
why: Three forks meeting at Banks give the Main (II-III), South Fork Canyon (IV) and the North Fork (V), all roadside and an hour from Boise.
heads_up: North Fork is expert-only; summer heat and traffic on Hwy 55

name: Peaks to Portland
why: One of the oldest open-water swims in the world, from Peaks Island across Casco Bay to East End Beach, revived by the YMCA in 1982.
heads_up: 58-62F water, fog, boat traffic; fundraising minimum

name: Peʻahi (Jaws)
why: The world's benchmark big-wave venue, home of the Jaws Big Wave Championships.
heads_up: Tow/paddle experts only; private dirt-road access; spectators on cliff

name: Pemberton (Mount Mackenzie)
why: Whistler's drier neighbour with a large PVTA-built network (Mosquito Lake, Happy Trail, Cream Puff) and big alpine descents.
heads_up: 4WD to launch; strong summer valley winds; keep LZ gates closed for livestock

name: Peña de Bernal
why: One of the world's tallest monoliths, a long-established multipitch destination two hours from Querétaro city.
heads_up: South (town) face closed by the state; climb the permitted faces only

name: Penobscot River West Branch
why: McKay Station releases below Ripogenus Dam feed Exterminator and the Cribworks, the East's hardest commercially rafted rapid, under Mount Katahdin.
heads_up: Class V Cribworks; remote private logging roads

name: Pere Marquette River
why: Site of the first brown trout stocking in America and a National Wild and Scenic River with blue-ribbon steelhead and salmon runs.
heads_up: Flies-only section; crowded fall salmon run

name: Phoenix (South Mountain / Hawes)
why: South Mountain's National Trail and the Hawes and McDowell networks give Phoenix a large, well-mapped winter riding scene.
heads_up: Rocky and technical; ride early to avoid heat

name: Pico de Orizaba
why: Mexico's highest peak (5,636 m) is a classic introductory glacier climb from the Piedra Grande hut with established guides in Tlachichuca.
heads_up: Altitude; 4x4 access to the hut; crampons required

name: Pictured Rocks
why: The Chapel-Mosquito loop and 42-mile lakeshore section of the North Country Trail show off Lake Superior's sandstone cliffs.
heads_up: Cold water and long cliff stretches with no landings

name: Pigeon River
why: Walters powerhouse releases on a set schedule make the Upper Pigeon a dependable class III-IV with a cluster of outfitters on I-40 near the Smokies.
heads_up: Release-day only; crowded commercial traffic in summer

name: Pinnacles National Park
why: California's long-standing winter crag with hundreds of bolted spire routes, plus the High Peaks and talus cave hikes.
heads_up: Seasonal raptor closures Jan–Jul on some formations; soft rock

name: Pisgah / Brevard
why: Rooty, raw Appalachian backcountry singletrack (Black Mountain, Farlow Gap, Pilot Rock) that defines East Coast technical riding.
heads_up: Long climbs, wet rock and limited signage

name: Pistol River
why: Host of the Pistol River Wave Bash (AWT/IWT), widely called the most consistent wave-sailing spot on the US West Coast with strong summer northwesterlies.
heads_up: Fully powered 3.7 days; cold water and big surf

name: Playa del Carmen bull sharks
why: Pregnant bull sharks gather on the sand flats off Playa every winter, making it the Caribbean's established bull-shark dive with dedicated operators.
heads_up: Winter season only; large sharks at close range

name: Point Lobos (Whalers Cove)
why: A state marine reserve with the richest kelp forest diving in California, limited to 30 divers a day and booked out months ahead.
heads_up: Advance reservation required; cold; surge

name: Point of the Mountain (Flight Park)
why: The busiest training site in the US: a state recreation area dedicated to free flight with multiple schools, a south side flown mornings and a north side evenings.
heads_up: Very busy; south side AM, north side PM; midday thermals can be rowdy

name: Port Huron
why: Start of the Bayview Mackinac Race (since 1925) and the Boat Night festival at the head of Lake Huron.
heads_up: St. Clair River current; freighter traffic

name: Porteau Cove
why: A BC provincial park built for divers, with sunken vessels, artificial reefs and marked entry points on Howe Sound.
heads_up: Cold, silty bottom; night diving popular

name: Portland Bridge Swim (Willamette River)
why: An 11-mile swim under 12 bridges on the Willamette, the Northwest's marquee marathon swim and part of Portland's growing river-swimming culture.
heads_up: Escort kayak required; river traffic; water-quality checks

name: Powder Mountain
why: Over 8,000 skiable acres with capped ticket sales, cat skiing and a cult following for untracked snow days after a storm.
heads_up: Long, flat traverses; some terrain is bus- or cat-access only

name: Presidential Range / Mount Washington
why: The Presidential Traverse and Tuckerman Ravine trail up Mount Washington, backed by the AMC hut system, define Northeast hiking.
heads_up: Worst weather in America above treeline; sudden storms

name: Prince William Sound
why: Blackstone Bay and Harriman Fjord's tidewater glaciers, reached from Whittier or Valdez, are Alaska's most accessible glacier kayaking.
heads_up: Cold water, rapid weather changes, Whittier tunnel schedule

name: Progreso / Chuburna
why: Merida's kite coast, with 15-25 kn spring thermals, winter Nortes and IKO schools at Progreso and Chuburna.
heads_up: Nortes bring 30-40 kn and brown chop Nov-Mar

name: Puerto Escondido / Zicatela
why: The 'Mexican Pipeline', the heaviest beach break in the world and a big-wave tour stop, with La Punta nearby for learners.
heads_up: Deadly shorebreak and rips at Zicatela; rainy season afternoons

name: Puerto Vallarta (Los Arcos / Marietas)
why: Los Arcos marine park and the Marietas Islands have anchored Banderas Bay's dive industry for decades, with mantas, giant Pacific manta season and humpbacks in winter.
heads_up: Marietas visitor caps; variable visibility

name: Pukaskwa Coast (Lake Superior)
why: The Coastal Paddling Route from Hattie Cove down Superior's wildest shore is Ontario's expedition sea-kayak route with boat-shuttle return.
heads_up: Open Superior swell, cold water, multi-day commitment

name: Punta de Mita / La Lancha
why: Banderas Bay's consistent longboard-friendly reef, with established surf schools and boat access to El Faro and Anclote.
heads_up: Walk-in through private land to La Lancha; rocky bottom

name: Purgatory Bike Park
why: Lift-served downhill above Durango that complements the town's XC heritage.
heads_up: Short season; afternoon storms

name: Pyramid Lake
why: The only place to catch giant Lahontan cutthroat from a ladder in the surf; a tribal fishery with a cult following of fly anglers.
heads_up: Tribal permit required; season closes July to September; cold wind

name: Rae Lakes Loop / Kings Canyon
why: The 41-mile Rae Lakes Loop from Roads End is the Sierra's classic multi-day backpack and shares the JMT/PCT corridor.
heads_up: Wilderness permit quota; bear canisters required

name: Rangeley Lakes
why: Historic brook trout and landlocked salmon destination where Carrie Stevens tied the Gray Ghost; the Outdoor Sporting Heritage Museum anchors the tradition.
heads_up: Fly-fishing-only waters; black flies in June; season closes Sept 30 on many waters

name: Raystown Lake / Allegrippis Trails
why: IMBA-built 30+ mile Allegrippis flow network at Seven Points, one of the East's best beginner-to-intermediate destinations.
heads_up: Humid summers and ticks; camping fills on weekends

name: Red Mountain
why: One of Canada's oldest ski hills, 360-degree skiing off Granite and Grey mountains with famous tree runs and in-bounds cat skiing.
heads_up: Steep, unmarked glades; limited lodging

name: Red River Gorge
why: The East's premier sport climbing with thousands of steep Corbin sandstone routes, Miguel's Pizza, and a dedicated climbers' coalition owning crags.
heads_up: Humidity in summer; busy fall weekends

name: Red Rock Canyon
why: Thousands of sandstone sport, trad and long multipitch routes 20 minutes from Las Vegas; one of the most-visited climbing areas in the US.
heads_up: Timed-entry reservations on the Scenic Loop; no climbing after rain

name: Redwood National and State Parks
why: James Irvine, Fern Canyon and Tall Trees Grove are the defining walks among the world's tallest trees.
heads_up: Tall Trees permit; coastal fog and mud

name: Resurrection Bay
why: Alaska's established dive base, with charter operators running Resurrection Bay's walls, kelp, sea lions and wrecks and a dive shop in town.
heads_up: Drysuit essential; limited operators; weather

name: Revelstoke
why: 5,620 ft of vertical, the most in North America, with resort, cat and heli skiing from a single base, plus big-mountain enduro trails (Frisby Ridge, Mt Macpherson) and a gondola-accessed paragliding launch.
heads_up: Long runs with serious tree-well risk; strong summer thermals for pilots

name: Rifle Mountain Park
why: America's most concentrated hard limestone sport climbing, with steep 5.12-5.14 classics in a narrow city-run canyon.
heads_up: Day-use fee; few routes below 5.11

name: Rincon
why: The 'Queen of the Coast', California's most celebrated point break and home of the Rincon Classic.
heads_up: Very crowded on winter swells; cobblestone entry; limited roadside parking

name: Río Alseseca
why: Home of Big Banana Falls and the Alseseca Race; the Roadside and Big Banana sections make Tlapacoyan the hub of Mexican creek-boating, based at Aventurec.
heads_up: Expert-only; peak visiting season Oct-Jan

name: Río Copalita
why: Pacific-coast rafting from San José Alemania to La Bocana beach, run daily by Huatulco outfitters in the rainy and early-dry season.
heads_up: Gentle float in dry months; upper class III-IV only after rains

name: Río Filobobos
why: Beginner rafting past the El Cuajilote archaeological site, run commercially from Tlapacoyan alongside the harder Alseseca.
heads_up: Low water in spring dry season

name: Rio Grande Taos Box
why: Seventeen miles of class IV in an 800-foot basalt gorge from John Dunn Bridge, the Southwest's signature spring run.
heads_up: Snowmelt-dependent; no exits once committed

name: Rio Nexpa
why: Mainland Mexico's legendary long left point, with decades of surf-camp cabanas lining the rivermouth.
heads_up: Remote stretch of Highway 200; rocks and rips; heavy in summer

name: Río Pescados / Río Antigua (Jalcomulco)
why: Mexico's rafting capital: the Pescados section's 20-plus class III-IV rapids run year-round with a dozen outfitters based in Jalcomulco, and the upper Barranca Grande reaches class IV-V in rains.
heads_up: Rainy-season flows (Jun-Sep) raise difficulty; dry months more technical

name: Río Tampaón (Huasteca Potosina)
why: Turquoise class II-III rafting through the Santa María canyons, plus the Micos cascades, make Ciudad Valles Mexico's second rafting hub.
heads_up: Operators switch rivers when Jul-Oct rains push it too high

name: Rockaway Beach
why: New York City's only legal surf beach, subway-accessible with a dense surf shop, school and lifeguard infrastructure.
heads_up: Surfing only in designated zones; crowded; cold water outside summer

name: Rocktown
why: Georgia's Triple Crown bouldering venue on Pigeon Mountain with hundreds of iron-hard sandstone problems.
heads_up: Georgia Outdoor Recreation Pass required; hunting-season closures

name: Rodanthe / Waves (REAL)
why: REAL Watersports' campus in Waves is the largest kite and wing school in the US, with the Slick flats and the annual Triple-S Invitational.
heads_up: Crowded slick; summer winds lighter

name: Rogers Pass
why: The most storied ski-touring area in North America, in Glacier National Park under Parks Canada's winter permit system.
heads_up: Winter permit and park pass required; artillery-controlled avalanche zones

name: Rogue River (Wild & Scenic)
venueType: multi-day class III-IV Wild & Scenic river
why: Thirty-four miles from Grave Creek with Rainie Falls, Blossom Bar and riverside lodges; one of the original 1968 Wild & Scenic rivers with a permit lottery.
heads_up: Lottery permit May 15-Oct 15; Blossom Bar wraps boats

name: Rossland / Seven Summits
why: Home of the Seven Summits IMBA Epic ridge ride and a dense Kootenay Columbia trail network from the townsite.
heads_up: Seven Summits needs a shuttle and full-day commitment

name: Rouge River
why: Seven Sisters and Mushroom rapids an hour from Montreal make the Rouge Quebec's most-rafted river with multiple outfitter bases.
heads_up: Big spring flows; low by late summer

name: Rumney
why: New England's sport-climbing capital with 1,000+ bolted routes on Rattlesnake Mountain.
heads_up: Parking fills early; some crags closed for peregrines in spring

name: Russell Fork
why: October Flannagan Dam releases through the Breaks Interstate Park gorge draw expert paddlers for the Lord of the Fork race; class V drops like El Horrendo.
heads_up: October release weekends only; class V with serious consequences

name: Saguenay Fjord
why: Belugas and minkes in a 100-km fjord with launch points at L'Anse-Saint-Jean, Baie-Éternité and Tadoussac inside the Saguenay-St. Lawrence Marine Park.
heads_up: Operators close in October; strict distance rules for belugas

name: Salida / Monarch Crest
why: The Monarch Crest Trail along the Continental Divide is one of Colorado's most famous shuttle rides, with Salida's S-Mountain trails in town.
heads_up: Above 11,000 ft; lightning risk after noon

name: Salt River Canyon
why: Arizona's spring snowmelt run through a Sonoran canyon, with day trips from US 60 and a permitted multi-day wilderness section.
heads_up: Short March-April window; tribal and Forest Service permits

name: San Diego Bay
why: San Diego Yacht Club (America's Cup 1988-1995) and year-round 10-15 kn sea breeze make this the US West Coast's most consistent racing venue.
heads_up: Navy and commercial traffic in the channel

name: San Francisco Bay (St. Francis YC)
why: The Rolex Big Boat Series and the 2013 America's Cup were sailed on the Cityfront's 20-25 kn breeze and strong tides.
heads_up: Heavy wind, current and fog; cold water

name: San Juan Islands
why: Orca-watching by sea kayak off San Juan Island's west side, with the densest cluster of kayak outfitters on the West Coast and the Cascadia Marine Trail campsites.
heads_up: Strong tidal currents in Haro Strait; ferry logistics

name: San Juan River (Navajo Dam)
why: The Southwest's premier tailwater, with huge midge-feeding rainbows in the Quality Waters below Navajo Dam and year-round fishing.
heads_up: Crowded Quality Waters; tiny flies; quality-water special regs

name: San Miguel / Ensenada
why: Baja's historic right point, surfed since the 1950s and host of Mexico's oldest surf contests.
heads_up: Rocks and localism; winter northwest swell only

name: Sandy Ridge
why: BLM and IMBA-built bike-only system (Hide and Seek, Two Turntables) that became Portland's most-ridden destination.
heads_up: Full parking lots on weekends; one paved climb

name: Santa Barbara (Skyport / Elings Park)
venueType: mountain launch with coastal training hill
why: Year-round flying from the Santa Ynez front range with the Santa Barbara Soaring Association, Eagle Paragliding school and the Elings Park training hill.
heads_up: Sundowner winds and strong sea-breeze convergence; SBSA membership and site briefing required

name: Santa Cruz / Soquel Demo Forest
why: Home of Santa Cruz Bicycles with the Flow Trail and Braille at Demo Forest and the UCSC and Wilder Ranch networks.
heads_up: Long fire-road climb to the top of Demo; poison oak

name: Sayulita
why: Mexico's best-known beginner surf town, with dozens of surf and SUP schools and the Punta Sayulita Longboard Classic.
heads_up: Very crowded lineup; runoff water quality after rain

name: Schweitzer
why: Idaho's largest ski area, 2,900 acres of bowls and glades above Lake Pend Oreille with reliable Inland Northwest snowfall.
heads_up: Fog and low cloud are common

name: Scorpion Bay / San Juanico
why: Baja's iconic cluster of up to seven right points, delivering some of the longest rides in North America on south swells.
heads_up: Long dirt-road approach; needs south swell; limited supplies

name: Seaside Cove
why: The north Oregon coast's premier winter point setup, holding big northwest swells.
heads_up: Strong localism; heavy rocks; cold water

name: Sebastian Inlet
why: Florida's most famous wave, the First Peak jetty wedge that produced Slater, Hobgoods and decades of ESA contests.
heads_up: Jetty rocks and crowds; state park entry fee

name: Sedona
why: Red-rock technical riding (Hiline, Hangover, Highline) and the Sedona Mountain Bike Festival make it the Southwest winter standard.
heads_up: Exposure on cliff-edge trails; Red Rock Pass parking fee

name: Selway River
why: One launch per day in season keeps the Selway the most pristine class IV multi-day in the lower 48; the hardest permit to draw.
heads_up: Permit lottery; dangerous above 4 ft at Paradise

name: Seneca Rocks
why: The East's classic exposed multipitch trad fin, used by Army mountain troops in WWII and home to long-running guide services.
heads_up: Loose rock and exposure; thunderstorms

name: Shawangunks (The Gunks)
why: America's most historic trad crag with horizontal-roof classics and a century of climbing on Mohonk Preserve land.
heads_up: Daily preserve fee; very crowded fall weekends

name: Sheboygan
why: The 'Malibu of the Midwest', the Great Lakes' freshwater surf capital since the 1960s and home of EOS Surf, Wisconsin's first surf shop.
heads_up: Wind-driven swell only; near-freezing water with ice in winter

name: Shelf Road
why: Over 1,000 vertical limestone sport routes on sunny BLM land; Colorado's prime winter cragging.
heads_up: Dirt road; cactus and loose approach terrain

name: Sherman Island
why: The Delta's thermal wind machine; the Rio Vista Windsurfing Association and Sherman Island Kiteboarding Organization maintain levee launches used by Bay Area riders all summer.
heads_up: Tidal current and power lines near Baja Road launch; only approved launches

name: Shilshole Bay / Puget Sound
why: Seattle's 1,400-slip Shilshole Bay Marina and Corinthian/Seattle yacht clubs anchor Puget Sound's racing scene and the Round the County and Race Week fleets.
heads_up: Light summer wind; strong tides

name: Short Sand Beach / Oswald West
why: Oregon's classic learner cove inside Oswald West State Park, protected from wind by headlands on both sides.
heads_up: Half-mile walk-in through forest; cold water; busy summer parking

name: SilverStar Bike Park
why: Long-running Okanagan bike park with a gondola to the summit and a reputation for flow and jump trails.
heads_up: Season runs late June to September only

name: Silverton Mountain
why: One chairlift, guided-only for most of the season, no groomers and 13,487 ft summit heli drops: the purest expert ski area in the US.
heads_up: Avalanche gear required; guided days book out early

name: Sitka / Sandy Beach
why: The hub of Alaskan surfing, with a multi-generational local community on the only road-accessible break in town.
heads_up: Needs a large SW swell; frigid water; low-key secretive locals

name: Sixmile Creek
why: Three progressively harder canyons off the Seward Highway, with the Third Canyon regarded as class V and commercial rafting from Hope.
heads_up: Class V Third Canyon; cold glacial water

name: Skaha Bluffs
why: Over 1,000 sport routes in a sunny Okanagan provincial park; Western Canada's biggest sport-climbing destination.
heads_up: Parking gate closed mid-Nov to mid-Mar; summer heat

name: Skeena / Bulkley Rivers
why: The Skeena system including the Bulkley, Kispiox, Babine and Morice is the global capital of wild summer steelhead on the swing.
heads_up: Classified-water licences and non-resident restrictions; lodges book a year out; cold wet fall

name: Skykomish River
why: Boulder Drop is Washington's benchmark class IV+ and the Sky is the Seattle area's standard spring run from Index.
heads_up: Boulder Drop at high water is class V; cold snowmelt

name: Skyline Trail (Cape Breton Highlands)
why: The Cabot Trail's Skyline headland is the most-hiked trail in the Maritimes, famous for sunsets and moose.
heads_up: Paid parking reservations in season; coyotes, hike in groups

name: Skyline Trail (Jasper)
why: The 44 km Skyline from Maligne Lake is the Rockies' most popular multi-day ridge walk, with half its length above treeline.
heads_up: Campsite reservations open in January and sell out; weather exposure

name: Slave River (Rapids of the Drowned)
why: Four sets of enormous-volume rapids (100,000-250,000 cfs) with routes from beginner to class VI; home of the annual Slave River Paddlefest.
heads_up: Local guide strongly advised; silty water hides swimmers

name: Smith Rock
why: Birthplace of American sport climbing with over 1,800 routes in a state park; the Misery Ridge loop is an iconic day hike.
heads_up: Very crowded weekends; summer heat on the main wall

name: Snake River (Jackson Hole)
why: Native Snake River cutthroat on dry flies beneath the Tetons, with a long-established guide and fly-shop scene in Jackson.
heads_up: Runoff until July; braided channels require experienced rowing

name: Snake River Alpine Canyon
why: Big Kahuna and Lunch Counter below Jackson Hole make this the most-rafted section in the Rockies, served by a dozen outfitters.
heads_up: Huge June flows; busy commercial traffic

name: Snowbasin
why: 2002 Olympic downhill venue with 3,000 ft of vertical, big-mountain terrain and famously uncrowded slopes.
heads_up: Exposed upper mountain closes in high wind

name: Snowbird
why: Tram-served steep terrain, Mineral Basin and one of the longest seasons in the US, often into May.
heads_up: Interlodge road closures during avalanche control

name: Snowshoe Bike Park
why: UCI World Cup downhill venue and IMBA Silver Ride Center with one of the roughest lift-served tracks on the circuit.
heads_up: Rocks and roots; remote mountaintop resort

name: Socorro / Revillagigedo Islands
why: The Mexican Galapagos, a UNESCO site 250 miles south of Cabo reached only by liveaboard, famous for giant mantas, hammerheads, dolphins and humpbacks.
heads_up: Liveaboard only, 24-hour crossing, advanced certification

name: South Fork American River
why: The most-rafted river in the West, with Chili Bar and the Gorge sections and a dense outfitter base in Coloma-Lotus an hour from Sacramento.
heads_up: Crowded summer weekends; flows set by upstream releases

name: South Fork of the Snake
why: One of the West's great cutthroat rivers below Palisades Dam, with a famous salmonfly hatch and a full lodge economy.
heads_up: Flows dictated by irrigation releases; canyon stretch requires a float

name: South Holston River
why: The Southeast's premier tailwater, with thousands of wild browns per mile and a year-round sulphur hatch below South Holston Dam.
heads_up: TVA generation schedule; crowded weekends

name: South Padre Island (Laguna Madre)
why: The Lower Laguna Madre offers miles of waist-deep flats and 200+ windy days a year, with multiple schools and bay-side kite beaches.
heads_up: Spring-break crowds; summer wind lighter and hot

name: Spider Mountain Bike Park
why: Texas's only lift-served bike park and the Southern US winter gravity option, with year-round chairlift operations.
heads_up: Summer heat; limited vertical (350 ft)

name: Squamish Spit
why: Howe Sound's daily inflow thermal makes Squamish Canada's most reliable windsport venue, managed by the Squamish Windsports Society with rescue boat coverage.
heads_up: Society membership/day fee; cold glacial water; river current at the Spit

name: St. Petersburg
why: Tampa Bay's St. Petersburg Yacht Club hosts the Helly Hansen NOOD, world championships and the St. Pete-to-Havana history; the US Sailing Center is here.
heads_up: Summer thunderstorms; light wind

name: Steamboat
why: Trademarked Champagne Powder, legendary tree skiing and a ranch town that has produced more winter Olympians than any other in the US.
heads_up: Lower-angle terrain overall; expert steeps are limited

name: Steamer Lane / Santa Cruz
why: Home of the Santa Cruz Surfing Museum and the birthplace of mainland surfing, with Steamer Lane for experts and Cowell's for lessons and SUP surfing.
heads_up: Crowded, localised lineup at the Lane; cold water; cliff-jump entry

name: Steelhead Alley (Lake Erie)
why: The Lake Erie tributaries from Ohio to New York hold the densest steelhead run in the Great Lakes, with Elk and Walnut creeks the centrepieces.
heads_up: Combat fishing on weekends; flow-dependent; winter cold

name: Stevens Pass
why: Seattle's core powder mountain, night skiing, and a renowned lift-served bike park in summer.
heads_up: US-2 pass closures and parking fills early; bike park runs July-Sept

name: Stone Fort (Little Rock City)
why: The Southeast's benchmark bouldering area and host of the Triple Crown series, on the Montlake golf course property.
heads_up: Day fee at the golf clubhouse; closes in wet conditions

name: Stonington / Deer Isle (Maine Island Trail)
why: The Merchant Row islands are the heart of the 375-mile Maine Island Trail, the original US water trail with member campsites.
heads_up: Fog, tides and lobster-boat traffic; MITA membership for sites

name: Stowe
why: The 'Ski Capital of the East' on Mount Mansfield with the Front Four steeps and a classic New England ski town.
heads_up: Ice and cold; Vail-era crowds and parking fees

name: String Lake / Jackson Hole
why: Grand Teton's signature flatwater paddle beneath the Tetons, with Jackson Hole outfitters and NPS launch permits.
heads_up: NPS boat permit and AIS inspection required; cold water; bears

name: Sugarbush
why: Two mountains including Castlerock's unmanicured steeps in the Mad River Valley, a classic Vermont ski destination.
heads_up: Castlerock lift lines on powder days

name: Sugarloaf
why: The only lift-served above-treeline snowfields in the East and the region's largest continuous vertical.
heads_up: Brutal cold; remote 2.5 hr drive from Portland

name: Sullivan's Island (Station 28.5)
why: An offshore sandbar makes a protected cove at Station 28.5, the Lowcountry's established kite beach with a sister launch at Isle of Palms Third Avenue.
heads_up: Tide-dependent sandbar; summer wind is light

name: Sun Peaks
why: Canada's second-largest ski area by acreage across three mountains, with a Nancy Greene legacy and a lift-served bike park.
heads_up: Cold interior temperatures in January

name: Sun Valley
why: America's first destination ski resort (1936) and birthplace of the chairlift, with Bald Mountain's 3,400 ft of fall-line groomers, an IMBA Gold-level Ride Center and tandem flights off Baldy.
heads_up: Low natural snowfall, relies on snowmaking; altitude and strong summer thermals

name: Sund Rock (Hood Canal)
why: Hood Canal's best-known dive, a privately managed preserve with wolf eels, giant Pacific octopus and easy shore entry.
heads_up: Access fee and sign-in; cold water

name: Sunday River
why: Eight peaks and the East's most reliable snowmaking make it Maine's busiest destination resort.
heads_up: Spread-out base areas; ice in cold snaps

name: Sunset Beach
why: Long-standing Triple Crown venue and the North Shore's premier big, shifting reef peak.
heads_up: Strong rips and shifting peaks; 8-15 ft typical in season

name: Sunshine Village
why: Canada's longest non-glacial season on the Continental Divide, with Delirium Dive among the most serious inbounds terrain in the country.
heads_up: Delirium Dive requires transceiver, shovel, probe and partner

name: Superior Hiking Trail
why: The 300-mile SHT along Lake Superior's North Shore is the Midwest's flagship long-distance and section-hiking trail.
heads_up: Bugs in June; free first-come campsites only

name: Swami's
why: North County San Diego's signature reef point below the Self-Realization Fellowship, a consistent winter wave with a deep local surf culture.
heads_up: Heavy crowds; long staircase access; shallow reef at low tide

name: Swim Around Key West
why: A 12.5-mile circumnavigation of Key West held every June since 1977 with solo and relay divisions, one of the classic warm-water marathon swims.
heads_up: Heat, jellyfish, boat traffic; kayak escort required

name: Swim the Suck (Tennessee River Gorge)
why: A 10-mile downriver swim through the Tennessee River Gorge, a fixture on the World's Top 100 Open Water Swims list with mandatory kayak escorts.
heads_up: Kayak escort required; river current and barge traffic

name: Tahquitz & Suicide Rocks
why: The historic home of the Yosemite Decimal System, with classic moderate granite multipitch above Idyllwild.
heads_up: Long uphill approach; summer heat

name: Tallulah Gorge
why: Georgia Power releases a handful of spring and November weekends (500-700 cfs) into a 1,000-foot gorge; the Oceana slide is a Southeastern bucket-list drop.
heads_up: Release weekends only; 600-step stair carry into the gorge

name: Taos Ski Valley
why: Kachina Peak and the Ridge hike-to chutes give it a reputation as the toughest terrain in the Southwest, with a renowned ski school.
heads_up: 12,481 ft summit altitude; steep first lift view can intimidate

name: Tapalpa
why: Former Paragliding World Cup venue above the Jalisco highlands with multiple tandem operators and a long-standing winter XC scene.
heads_up: Altitude above 2,000 m; strong dry-season thermals

name: Tatshenshini-Alsek
why: Ten-day raft expedition from Dalton Post through the world's largest protected wilderness to Alsek Bay's icebergs; the Alsek's Turnback Canyon is a famed class V+ portage.
heads_up: Permit lotteries (Alsek via Parks Canada, Tat via BC Parks); grizzlies and cold

name: Telluride
why: A box-canyon mining town with free gondola access to 4,400 ft of vertical and Palmyra Peak hike-to terrain, lift-served summer trails, and the Telluride Festival of Flight from 12,000 ft Gold Hill.
heads_up: Remote: long drives or small-plane flights; narrow valley with limited LZs for pilots

name: Ten Sleep Canyon
why: A 20 km Bighorn limestone canyon with 1,000+ pocketed sport routes and a thriving summer camping scene.
heads_up: No new bolting since 2019 USFS order; afternoon storms

name: Teton Pass
why: The most famous roadside backcountry skiing in the US, with the Mount Glory bootpack from the summit lot, and in summer the Lithium, Jimmy's Mom and Black Canyon descents that anchor Jackson Hole mountain biking.
heads_up: Avalanche terrain, no patrol, lot fills by 7am on powder days; steep exposed trails in grizzly country

name: The Enchantments
why: The 18-mile Enchantments traverse via Aasgard Pass is the Pacific Northwest's most coveted alpine hike and backpacking permit.
heads_up: Overnight lottery; Aasgard Pass is steep and exposed

name: The Needles (Black Hills)
why: Custer State Park's granite needles are a runout-trad heritage area pioneered by Herb and Jan Conn and Fritz Wiessner.
heads_up: Bold, sparsely protected routes; park entry fee

name: Third Avenue (Foster City)
why: The South Bay's flat-water kite and wing launch with the most consistent afternoon thermals on the peninsula.
heads_up: Shallow mud at low tide; crowded car park

name: Thompson River
why: Jaws of Death and the Frog in a dry canyon at the Fraser confluence; BC's highest-volume commercial rafting run.
heads_up: Huge summer volume; Lytton recovering from 2021 wildfire

name: Thousand Islands
why: 1,800 islands in the St. Lawrence between Clayton NY and Gananoque ON, with the Thousand Islands Water Trail and outfitters on both shores.
heads_up: Freighter traffic in the shipping channel; border crossing by water

name: Thunder Bay National Marine Sanctuary
why: Nearly 100 known shipwrecks in cold, clear Lake Huron, protected by a NOAA sanctuary with mooring buoys, glass-bottom tours and shallow wrecks for snorkellers.
heads_up: Cold freshwater; drysuit recommended

name: Thunder Mountain Bike Park
why: Gravity Logic-built lift-served park at Berkshire East with the longest flow trails in southern New England.
heads_up: Mostly weekends outside peak summer

name: Tiger Mountain / Poo Poo Point
why: Seattle's home site with two groomed launches, a club LZ and Seattle Paragliding school; among the busiest sites in the Pacific Northwest.
heads_up: Northwest Paragliding Club membership; hikers on launch; afternoon valley wind

name: Tobermory / Fathom Five
why: Canada's first national marine park, with 22 shipwrecks in gin-clear Georgian Bay water and a dive-town infrastructure built around them.
heads_up: Cold water; park registration fee; strict mooring rules

name: Tofino / Cox Bay
why: Canada's surf capital, with over a dozen surf schools (Surf Sister since 2003), Rip Curl Pro Tofino and 35 km of surfable beach.
heads_up: Cold water year-round (5/4 suit); summer afternoon NW wind

name: Tombstone Territorial Park (Grizzly Lake)
why: The Grizzly, Divide and Talus Lakes route on the Dempster Highway is the Yukon's signature backcountry hike.
heads_up: Campsite permits required; bears and no cell coverage

name: Toronto Harbour / RCYC
why: Lake Ontario's biggest racing fleet, anchored by the Royal Canadian Yacht Club (founded 1852) and the Lake Ontario 300.
heads_up: Ferry and boat traffic in the inner harbour; cold water until July

name: Torrey Pines Gliderport
why: The oldest continuously operating flight park in North America, with on-site school, tandems and reliable sea-breeze ridge lift over 300 ft cliffs.
heads_up: Ridge-soaring only; crowded airspace with tandems, hang gliders and RC; sea breeze must be on

name: Traversee du lac Memphremagog (Magog)
why: The Newport-to-Magog international marathon swim, run since 1979 and part of the WOWSA Ultramarathon series, with shorter public distances.
heads_up: Cross-border swim; cold north wind

name: Traversee du lac St-Jean
why: The 32 km Peribonka-to-Roberval crossing has run every July since 1955, a FINA Grand Prix and WOWSA Ultramarathon series race that is the heart of a week-long festival.
heads_up: Invitation-level pros; cold, wind-driven lake

name: Tsali Recreation Area
why: Classic lakeside loop system on Fontana Lake that has been a Southeast MTB staple since the 1990s.
heads_up: Alternating bike/horse days on the loops

name: Tuckerman Ravine
why: America's original spring-skiing pilgrimage: a 2.4-mile hike from Pinkham Notch to a 50-degree headwall on Mount Washington.
heads_up: Avalanches, falling ice and crevasses; no lifts, hike everything

name: Tucson
why: Winter training base with Tucson Mountain Park, 50-Year Trail, Mt Lemmon descents and the 24 Hours in the Old Pueblo race.
heads_up: Cactus and rocky terrain; summer heat is dangerous

name: Tuolumne Meadows
why: Yosemite's high-country domes offer classic knob-and-slab granite multipitch at 8,600 ft with cool summer temps and JMT/PCT access.
heads_up: Tioga Road closed roughly Nov–May; afternoon storms

name: Tuolumne River
why: Eighteen miles of class IV from Meral's Pool with Clavey Falls, California's premier advanced multi-day near Yosemite.
heads_up: Forest Service permit; rough Lumsden Road access

name: Two Step (Honaunau Bay)
why: The Big Island's best shore snorkel and dive, a lava-step entry beside Pu'uhonua o Honaunau with coral gardens, turtles and spinner dolphins.
heads_up: Slippery lava entry; limited parking; respect the heiau

name: U.S. National Whitewater Center
why: The world's largest recirculating whitewater channel and a US Olympic training site, with class II-IV channels running most of the year.
heads_up: Pumped channel, day-pass pricing; competition closures

name: Upper Animas
why: Twenty-six miles of continuous class IV-V from Silverton with railroad take-out, the Rockies' classic multi-day expert run.
heads_up: 9,000 ft altitude, cold water, train-only egress

name: Upper Delaware River
why: The best wild-trout dry-fly river in the East, with the West Branch tailwater, large selective browns and a strong guide scene.
heads_up: Highly selective fish; limited wading; release-dependent flows

name: Upper Youghiogheny
why: Deep Creek Lake releases on set weekdays produce a steep, continuous class IV-V run that is the East's standard advanced summer river.
heads_up: Release days only (typically Mon/Fri/Sat); technical and continuous

name: USS Oriskany
why: The largest vessel ever sunk as an artificial reef, a 900-ft aircraft carrier 22 miles off Pensacola that anchors the Florida Panhandle Shipwreck Trail.
heads_up: Flight deck at 145 ft, strong current, long boat ride; technical for most of the wreck

name: Vail
why: The Back Bowls and Blue Sky Basin give 5,000-plus acres on one of the most recognised ski mountains in the world.
heads_up: High prices and heavy crowds during holidays

name: Val-David / Val-Morin
why: The birthplace of Quebec climbing, with Mont Césaire, Condor and King in a regional park an hour from Montreal.
heads_up: Some Mont-Césaire sectors closed over land disputes; check access

name: Valdez / Thompson Pass
why: Birthplace of big-mountain heli-skiing and the World Extreme Skiing Championships in the Chugach spine country.
heads_up: Heli-only or committing tours; BLM permit review ongoing

name: Valle de Bravo
why: North America's winter XC paragliding capital (Monarca Open and Paragliding World Cup at El Peñón), Mexico's inland sailing capital with 300-boat regattas on the daily thermal, and the Monte Alto trail network for riders.
heads_up: Altitude (1,800-2,300 m); thermals and wind only after noon; busy launch in peak season

name: Vallee Bras-du-Nord
why: Purpose-built cooperative trail network (Neilson sector) north of Quebec City that has become Quebec's flagship enduro and flow destination.
heads_up: Day-use fee; cold and buggy in June

name: Vantage / Frenchman Coulee
why: Eastern Washington's dry-side basalt columns are the region's go-to shoulder-season sport and crack destination.
heads_up: Loose rock and high wind; blistering summer heat

name: Vedauwoo
why: The spiritual home of offwidth and wide-crack climbing on coarse Sherman granite.
heads_up: Check USFS road gate status; skin-shredding rock

name: Victoria (Swiftsure)
why: The Swiftsure International Yacht Race (since 1930) starts off Clover Point and sends 130+ boats into the Strait of Juan de Fuca each May.
heads_up: Strong tides and shipping in the strait

name: Virginia Beach / 1st Street Jetty
why: Host of the East Coast Surfing Championships, the longest-running surf contest in the world, held every August since 1963.
heads_up: Summer surfing restrictions on the main beach; small summer surf

name: Waddell Creek
why: The mainland's original wave-sailing arena (national contests 1985-2000, Santa Cruz Goya Windsurfing Festival) with side-onshore NW wind right off Highway 1.
heads_up: Cold water, sharks, wave priority rules

name: Waikiki
why: The cradle of modern surfing and of stand-up paddling, where beach boys have taught Queens and Canoes for over a century; the Waikiki Roughwater Swim (since 1970) inspired the Ironman swim leg.
heads_up: Very crowded; long paddle to outer breaks; reef underfoot

name: Wailua River
why: Hawaii's only navigable river, paddled to Secret Falls by permitted outfitters year-round.
heads_up: Permit-limited operators; closed Sundays for rentals

name: Waimea Bay
why: The birthplace of big-wave surfing and home of the Eddie Aikau Invitational, which runs only when faces exceed 40 ft.
heads_up: Only breaks on giant swells; dangerous shorebreak even for swimmers

name: Walden Pond
why: Thoreau's pond is New England's best-known open-water training venue, with a DCR-designated swim lane and a half-mile crossing swum daily in season.
heads_up: Swim buoy mandatory, restricted hours during lifeguard season, parking caps

name: Wenatchee River
why: Washington's most-rafted river, with warm high-volume class III from Leavenworth to Cashmere in early summer.
heads_up: Short snowmelt window; busy commercial season

name: West Coast Trail
why: Pacific Rim's ladders, cable cars and beach walks make the West Coast Trail one of the world's great coastal backpacks.
heads_up: Permits and mandatory orientation; tides, mud and injuries common

name: West Dennis Beach
why: Cape Cod's main kite beach, with a designated kite zone at the west end and the same SW sea breeze as Kalmus.
heads_up: Summer beach restrictions; paid parking

name: Westport
why: Washington's surf town, with the state's main surf shops, schools, and the long-running Cleanwater Classic contest at the Westhaven jetty.
heads_up: Cold water (hoods and booties); strong jetty currents

name: Westwater Canyon
why: The Colorado's one-day black-rock gorge with Skull Rapid; BLM permit lottery and a Moab outfitter staple.
heads_up: BLM permit required; Skull's Room of Doom eddy

name: Whistler Blackcomb
why: The largest ski resort in North America (2010 Olympic host, over a mile of vertical) and the world's benchmark lift-served bike park (A-Line, Dirt Merchant, Top of the World) with Crankworx every summer and Alta Lake paddling.
heads_up: Big crowds, coastal rain at the village in warm storms

name: White River (Bull Shoals)
why: The 'Trout Capital of the USA' tailwater below Bull Shoals Dam, known for world-record brown trout and a huge resort and guide economy.
heads_up: Generation schedules change flows hourly; boat-dependent

name: White Salmon River
why: Spring-fed year-round flows through a narrow basalt gorge from BZ Corner, with Husum Falls as the highest commercially rafted drop in the US.
heads_up: Husum Falls is optional class V; cold water

name: Whiteface
why: Two-time Olympic venue with the greatest vertical drop in the East (3,430 ft) and the Slides backcountry zone.
heads_up: Notoriously icy and cold; the Slides open only in good conditions

name: Whitefish Mountain
why: Big Mountain's rime-coated 'snow ghost' trees and 3,000 acres next to Glacier National Park make it Montana's other must-ski.
heads_up: Frequent fog and flat light on the upper mountain

name: Whitewater
why: Ymir Bowl powder, 40 ft of Kootenay snow and a slackcountry culture that draws skiers worldwide to Nelson.
heads_up: Small lift system; avalanche gear for slackcountry

name: Whytecliff Park
why: Canada's first saltwater marine protected area and Vancouver's signature shore dive, with the Cut and the Plumose Wall minutes from the city.
heads_up: Cold; parking fills early; the Cut drops steeply

name: Williams Lake
why: Self-styled shuttle capital of BC with 200+ km of Fox Mountain and Westsyde singletrack maintained by the Williams Lake Cycling Club.
heads_up: Remote; bring shuttle logistics and bear awareness

name: Windrock Bike Park
why: Shuttle-run downhill park that hosts pro GRT and national downhill races and is the Southeast's go-to for steep, rough gravity riding.
heads_up: Expert-level DH; permit and shuttle fees

name: Winter Park
why: Mary Jane's bump runs are a Colorado institution, and Trestle Bike Park is one of the biggest lift-served parks in the US.
heads_up: Berthoud Pass road closures in storms

name: Witless Bay / Bay Bulls
why: Icebergs, humpbacks and the largest puffin colony in North America, kayaked from Bay Bulls outfitters half an hour from St. John's.
heads_up: Icebergs can roll; cold Labrador Current water

name: Wolf Creek
why: The most snow in Colorado, around 430 inches a year, on a no-frills, family-owned pass-top mountain.
heads_up: No lodging at the base; pass road closes in storms

name: Woodrat Mountain
why: BLM-managed flight site with two launches, hosts the Rat Race and other national competitions, and is home to the Rogue Valley Hang Gliding and Paragliding Association.
heads_up: Strong midday thermals; landing fields are private with club agreements; snow on upper road in winter

name: Woodstock (Blue Ridge)
why: The Mid-Atlantic's classic ridge-soaring and XC site on Massanutten with the Capitol Hang Gliding and Paragliding Association.
heads_up: CHGPA membership; strong northwest ridge days; LZ etiquette

name: Wrightsville Beach
why: Home of the Carolina Cup, once the largest SUP race in the world, plus a century-old surf scene with the Wrightsville Beach Surf Camp and Graveyard course.
heads_up: Summer crowds and paid parking; hurricane season

name: Xcalak / Chetumal Bay
why: Southern Yucatan permit, bonefish and tarpon flats with established lodges on the Costa Maya and inside Chetumal Bay.
heads_up: Remote, long drive from Cancun; wind

name: Yakima River Canyon
why: Washington's only Blue Ribbon trout stream with a full guide and fly-shop economy two hours from Seattle.
heads_up: High summer irrigation flows; wild-trout catch and release

name: Yakutat / Cannon Beach
why: Alaska's best-known surf town, with a surf shop operating since 1999 and ten miles of swell-exposed beach.
heads_up: Fly-in only; cold water (6/5 suit); bears on the beach

name: Yellowstone River (Paradise Valley)
why: The longest undammed river in the lower 48 with a legendary summer hopper float through Paradise Valley and a historic fly-shop town in Livingston.
heads_up: Runoff blows it out until early July; wind in Paradise Valley

name: Yosemite Valley
why: Birthplace of American big-wall climbing (El Capitan, Half Dome, Camp 4) with thousands of routes and the busiest Mountain Project area in the country.
heads_up: Crowds and reservations; summer heat on the walls

name: Yukon River (Whitehorse to Dawson)
why: The 715-km Whitehorse-to-Dawson run is the classic northern river expedition and the course of the Yukon River Quest paddling race each June.
heads_up: Two-week self-supported trip; Lake Laberge wind and cold water

name: Zion National Park
why: Moonlight Buttress and Touchstone are America's sandstone big-wall classics, while Angels Landing and The Narrows are among the most famous hikes on earth.
heads_up: Angels Landing permit lottery; flash floods in The Narrows
